text.content:
You type four commands yourself (status, tag, distill and promote); the follow-up runs by itself after a PASS, and the engineer sets things up and fixes what breaks.
A practice copy of the editor feedback loop: its own rulebook (one tag) and 9 real claims that you review in a Claims table like the real one. Nothing here changes the real tables or Geo. Do the steps in order; you can stop after any step and come back. Commands go into Claude Code, opened in the geo-agents folder. Commands act on the newest practice page under Onboarding; if one was made after yours, ask the engineer before you continue.

Rule 3 of Context-dependent says that a descriptive definite which names a kind of thing but not which one ("the Bitcoin ETF", "the new model") makes the claim Context-dependent: the reader must already know which one is meant. Editors read it with two gaps: a group every reader knows by its standing role, such as the press pool, is identified, and a capitalised phrase that names no body readers know, such as the AI Force, is not.
The press pool was justified in suspending coverage…
The AI Force should enforce binding safety standards
Can't tell: a name, or a kind?
The USPS ballot portal should not launch before the 2026…
No tag: USPS says which one
Georgia's gubernatorial debate should be moderated by…
No tag: it names its place
No tag: the claim reads well

The four are yours: you decide them in Your queue, the agent reads your decisions and drafts a clearer rule 3 from the ones that blame the rule, you approve it, and a safety check makes sure the earlier decisions still come out right before the new rule is used. They show the ways a decision can go: the press pool and the AI Force blame rule 3, the USPS claim blames the agent, and on the Georgia claim you agree with the agent.

The four claims were picked for the demo: the agent is fairly sure of three of them, but the page marks all four To review, so their Agent status reads Waits for you and all four sit in Your queue. The AI Force claim is the one the agent reads differently from run to run. For real, a claim waits when someone marks it To review or when the agent is unsure.
Check that the demo is set up and see what waits for whom.

Rulebook: 1 tag, Context-dependent, edition 2026-10-27.1 (an edition is a date plus a count; it goes up when a rule changes). Claims: 9 rows, Agent tags empty; 5 are Reviewed, decided earlier by an editor, and 4 are To review, for you. Agent reading holds a line on each of the 5 earlier decisions and nothing on yours. Rule changes: empty. Nothing is paused.
No table changes. Claude replies with one sentence, this table and a "Next:" line:

The sentence starts with "Demo · " and names this practice page, as every report in the demo does, and says that nothing waits for you yet: Your queue lists a claim only once the agent has read it, and the agent has not read the claims yet. The Next line points at step 2.
Step 2 · The agent reads the claims
The agent reads the 9 claims against the rulebook and writes its columns on every claim, your 4 included.

Your 4 claims, the press pool, the AI Force, the USPS claim and the Georgia claim, are To review and the agent has written nothing on them; the agent's columns (Agent tags, Agent confidence, Agent reasons, Agent status, Tags waiting, Agent edition and Agent remarks) are empty on all 9 claims, and Agent reading is empty on your 4 (step 1).
. It is a short wait; Notion changes only at the end.

Tags waiting names the tags that wait for you, Agent reading is still empty because the agent reads a decision only after you have made it, and Agent reasons holds one line for each tag the agent judged: the tag, the reason, the rule it cites (when it cites one) and how many of its readings agree. For your 4 claims, as one run read them:
The press pool was justified in suspending coverage…
Context-dependent: "the press pool": which one? · Context-dependent rule 3 · 1 of 1 runs agree
The AI Force should enforce binding safety standards

A claim the agent is sure of is read once, so its line ends with a count of one; the agent reads a claim again only when it is unsure, and a third time only when the first two readings disagree. The figures differ from run to run, and the AI Force claim most of all: the agent may read it as Can't tell, as here, or answer with confidence either way, and then its line may cite a rule or none. All four claims are To review, so each waits for you whatever the agent reads: Agent tags stays empty on all four, Agent status reads Waits for you and Tags waiting holds the tag. All four are now in Your queue, lowest confidence first. Agent confidence is the lowest confidence among the tags the agent judged on a claim. The agent agrees with all 5 earlier decisions: their Agent tags are the tags an editor confirmed, their Agent status is Done and their Tags waiting is empty. Agent edition holds 2026-10-27.1 on all 9 claims, and Agent remarks stays empty, because the rulebook has no tag that was left unchecked.
Step 3 · Decide your four claims (you, as the editor)
Record your decision on each of the four claims. You say whether the tag applies and add a note; the agent reads the reason from your decision in step 4.

All four of your claims are To review and wait in Your queue (step 2): Agent status reads Waits for you on all four, Tags waiting holds Context-dependent, Agent tags is empty and Agent reading is empty.

Fill in three columns on each of your four claims, in the order of its list, in Your queue under the lists. The sentence for Challenged tags notes stands on its own line between quotes: paste the words between the quotes, not the quotes. Review status comes last because it closes the claim. A claim leaves Your queue as soon as you set Review status to Reviewed. On the real Claims table the agent judges several tags: keep the Agent tags you agree with in Verified tags.

Challenged tags notes: paste the words between the quotes:
"Rule 3 does not say that a capitalised phrase which names no body readers know, such as the AI Force, is still a kind of thing and not which one; it is: the claim needs context."
Verified tags: leave it empty, because the tag does not apply.

"Rule 3 does not say that a group every reader knows by its standing role, such as the press pool, counts as identified; it does: the claim reads well."

"Agent slip. USPS names which portal, so rule 5 already settles it."

Challenged tags notes: leave it empty. An empty note is a decision too: you agree with the agent.

A note that starts with "Agent slip.", "Rule unclear." or "Rule should change." is taken as it stands and the agent does not read that tag; without one the agent reads your decision itself. If you disagree with the agent and leave the note empty, the agent still reads your decision, marks its reading "without your note", lists the claim in Needs your note and drafts nothing from it until you add a note.

Step 4 · The agent reads your decisions and drafts a clearer rule 3
Let the agent read each of your decisions, then turn the ones that blame rule 3 into one proposed rewording of rule 3.
Rule changes is empty; Agent reading is empty on your 4 claims, and your decisions are in (step 3).

A reading is the agent's own answer to why a decision differs from its tag. It is one of three: Agent slip (the rule as written settles it your way and the agent misread it), Rule unclear (the rule can honestly be read both ways on this claim) or Rule should change (the rule as written decides against you). It names the rule and gives one line of why. Only the readings that blame the rule, Rule unclear and Rule should change, become a draft.
Claude's report counts what was read, what points at a rule, the agent's slips and the decisions without a note, and its Next line opens Lessons waiting.
The press pool was justified in suspending coverage…

Nothing to read: the agent agreed with you.

The agent may read either claim as Rule unclear or as Rule should change; the draft is the same either way. The USPS claim is read at once, because your note opens with "Agent slip." and the agent takes your word; the Georgia claim has nothing to read. The 5 earlier decisions carry a reading too, put there when this page was made: Agent slip, with the note "Seeded from the audit of 9 October."

Current text holds today's rule 3. Proposed text keeps it and adds what the notes on the press pool and the AI Force claim say, for example: "A group readers know by its standing role, such as a press corps, counts as identified; a capitalised phrase that names no body readers know does not." Supporting rows lists the claims the draft rests on, the press pool and the AI Force, one line each (the table shows the first). The USPS claim drafts nothing: it blames the agent, not the rule, and stays an earlier decision. Each Supporting rows line ends with the claim's id and the tag; you can skip it.
The Rulebook does not change: a draft changes nothing until you approve it and it passes the safety check.
Step 5 · Approve the draft (you, as the rule owner)
Decide whether the draft may be tested; approving does not change the rule yet.
The draft from step 4 is Proposed.

In Lessons waiting, just below, read Current text and Proposed text side by side; the cells wrap, so you read both in place. If the draft says what you meant, set Status to Approved right there. If not, open the row, write all of rule 3 as you want it in Editor wording, then set Status to Approved; your wording is tested instead of the draft.
Known groups count as identified, unknown names do not
Test the approved rule 3 against everything already decided, and switch to it only if nothing breaks.
The Rulebook still has today's rule 3; the change is Approved (step 5).

. This is the longest wait of the seven steps: the agent reads the 10 example claims, the earlier decisions (the 5 from the audit, and your USPS and Georgia claims) and the press pool and AI Force claims the draft rests on, once with each version of rule 3, and twice more any claim whose answer differs between the two versions. When the check passes, the same command re-checks the claims the draft rests on (step 7).

When the check passes, Claude's report says PASS in its sentence, its table counts what came out right (the example claims, the earlier decisions and the claims the draft rests on), and its Next line points at step 7. These tables change:
Today's rule, plus: "a group known by its role is identified; an unknown name-like phrase is not."
Known groups count as identified, unknown names do not

The press pool and the AI Force claim are now earlier decisions too: every future safety check tests a new rule against them. The check counts only the earlier decisions the agent had right before the change, which is why the USPS claim, where the agent slipped, is not in the count.

Rule changes shows Status Approved and a Safety check result such as "FAIL: 'Excluding CNN from Air Force One violates the federal court…' now Does not apply". The Rulebook is unchanged. Claude's report says FAIL in its sentence and quotes that claim; its Next line hands you the whole text for Editor wording: the rule as it was tested, with a sentence written from that claim added at the end. For example, the added sentence reads: "A definite that names one particular order, case or document the claim does not identify still makes the claim Context-dependent."

Open the change in Lessons waiting. Editor wording must hold all of rule 3: put the whole text the report gives you into it (the rule as it was tested, with the added sentence at the end), or write all of rule 3 as you want it. Edit the added sentence if it does not say what you mean. You may also reject the change.
If it fails again, set Status to Rejected. The rule stays as it was, the demo ends here, and the safety check has done its job.

The same three steps apply when the check names one of your own claims instead of an example claim: the Safety check result then reads like "FAIL: 'The press pool was justified in suspending coverage…' now Applies", and the report proposes a sentence for that claim in the same way.
Step 7 · The agent re-checks your claims
Confirm that the agent now agrees with the decisions the rule change rests on, the press pool and the AI Force claim, and see that the other two wait for the next tag run.

You decided all four claims in step 3 and the new rule 3 went live in step 6; in step 2 all four claims waited for you, so the agent had written no tag on any of them, and all four still read Waits for you in Agent status.

Nothing to type: the follow-up ran by itself at the end of the safety check. It takes the answers the check already gave for the claims the draft rests on, under the new rule 3, so there was nothing more to wait for. Open the Claims table among the tables just below.

Agent tags now holds the tags you decided on the press pool and the AI Force claim: the AI Force claim carries the tag and the press pool claim does not. Agent status reads Done on both; neither claim says Disagrees with your decision, and a claim that did would show up in Agent disagreed and would need a clearer rule. Agent edition names the next edition, the one the safety check put in force, and Agent confidence follows the new reading. The USPS and Georgia claims were not part of the change, so the follow-up leaves them as they were: they keep Waits for you in Agent status until the next tag run reads them again, and they are not in Your queue, because you set them Reviewed in step 3. Only the claims the change rests on name the new edition: the other two and the 5 earlier decisions keep theirs until the next tag run. That is one full cycle: the agent read your decisions, the notes that blamed rule 3 became a clearer rule 3, it was tested against every earlier decision before it went live, and the press pool and AI Force claims are earlier decisions now, checked by every future safety check.
What the full version adds later:
All 13 tags are judged, not only Context-dependent.
Duplicates are found by searching all claims.
Each editor gets a queue of their own when more editors join.
When you are done, leave this page under Onboarding; it does no harm.

text.content: : one row per claim, shaped like the real claims table. The agent writes Agent tags, Agent confidence, Agent reasons, Agent status, Tags waiting, Agent edition, Agent remarks and Agent reading; you write Verified tags, Review status and Challenged tags notes.
: the agent's own record of each decision; nothing to do here.

Hover over a column name to see what it means.

Name.description: The tag's name; one row per tag.

Counterpart.description: The opposite tag it pairs with (Self-contained for Context-dependent).

Description.description: One or two sentences describing a claim that carries the tag.

Evidence.description: The report the tag's verification rests on.

Example Claims.description: Claims that show the tag, one per line.

Geo Status.description: Whether the tag exists in Geo.

Polarity.description: Kept as in the taxonomy; the agent does not use it.

When to use.description: The numbered rules the agent applies; a tag is judged only when this holds rules.

Work tags.description: The work the tag belongs to; every row here has Issue.

Agent confidence.description: How sure the agent is: the lowest confidence among the tags it judged on the claim, from 0.5 (a coin flip) to 1 (certain). Your queue is sorted by it, lowest first.

Agent reasons.description: Why the agent proposed what it did: one line per judged tag, "<Tag>: <reason> · <rule cited> · <k> of <n> runs agree", so you can decide without opening the agent's record.

Agent status.description: What the agent says about the claim: Waits for you (a tag needs your decision), Done, Disagrees with your decision, or Could not read. Your queue lists Waits for you until you set Review status to Reviewed.

Agent edition.description: The rulebook edition the agent wrote this row under.

Agent remarks.description: What the agent could not check, such as "not checked: 6 tags without rules"; empty when it checked everything.

Agent reading.description: What the agent made of your decision, one line per tag where you differed from it: Agent slip, Rule unclear or Rule should change, the rule, and why. Empty until the agent has read your decision.

Review status.description: To review or Reviewed. A claim is decided once it is Reviewed; anything else leaves it open. Set it last: the claim leaves Your queue as soon as it is Reviewed.

Challenged tags notes.description: Your words. A line that starts with a tag name and a colon belongs to that tag. Open it with Agent slip, Rule unclear or Rule should change and a full stop to say what you think went wrong; otherwise the agent reads it. "rule 4" names the rule.

Geo ID.description: The claim's identity in Geo; the queue's Key starts with it.

Geo Space.description: The Geo space the claim was read from.

Geo Created.description: The day the claim was made in Geo.

Geo Sources.description: The claim's sources, as Geo lists them.

Geo Is factual.description: Ticked when Geo marks the claim as factual.

Key.description: The claim's Geo ID, two colons, the tag; one row per claim and tag.

Tag.description: The tag the row is about.

Agent confidence.description: How sure the agent is of its answer, from 0.5 (a coin flip) to 1 (certain); the queue is sorted by it, lowest first.

Agent reason.description: At most 40 words, then the rule cited and how many runs agreed.

Claim link.description: Link to the claim's row in the Claims table.

Rulebook edition.description: The edition the proposal was made under.

Follow-up.description: Set after a safety check PASS, on the rows the change rests on.

Tag outcome.description: Copied by the agent from the claim once an editor has Reviewed it: Applies when the tag is in Verified tags, else Does not apply.

Why wrong.description: Copied by the agent from your note on the claim: the reason word that opens the tag's line (Agent slip, Rule unclear or Rule should change), for a tag whose outcome differs from the proposal.

Your reasoning.description: Copied by the agent from Challenged tags notes: the tag's own line, else the whole text.

Decided under.description: The edition the proposal you saw was made under, recorded when the agent copies your decision from the claim.

Agent reading.description: What the agent made of your decision where you differed from it: Agent slip (the rule settles it your way), Rule unclear (it reads both ways) or Rule should change (it decides against you). Written by the agent.

Rule.description: The rule the reading points at, for example "Context-dependent rule 3".

Reading note.description: One line of why. It opens with "without your note" when you wrote nothing for the tag.

Read under.description: The edition and a short mark of what the reading rests on: your decision, your note and the proposal the agent made. The agent reads a row again only when one of those changes.

Lesson.description: A short name for the change.

Tag.description: The tag the change is about.

Safety check result.description: For example "PASS: examples 11/11, earlier 10/10, yours 2/2" or "FAIL: 'Excluding CNN from Air Force One violates the federal court order' now Does not apply".

Supporting rows.description: One line per decided row the change rests on: the claim shortened, " · ", the row's Key.

Editor wording.description: The rule as the editor words it; when filled, the safety check tests it instead of the Proposed text. Never written by the agent.

Status.description: The editor sets Approved and Rejected; the agent sets Proposed, Live and Rolled back.

Paused.description: Ticked by a person, every command then refuses; cleared by a person.

Rulebook edition.description: The edition in force: a date plus a count, such as 2026-10-16.1; it goes up when a rule changes.

Last run summary.description: One short line, such as "Promote · 16 Oct 11:20 · PASS".

properties.Name: Context-dependent
properties.Description: A claim whose meaning depends on something introduced outside it: a pronoun or a definite reference ("the initiative", "the vulnerabilities", "recent actions") that no name inside the claim resolves, so a reader cannot tell what it points at.
properties.Example Claims:
Open AI's initiative went well with the target group.
He said the new model outperforms its predecessor.
The company's revenue grew 40% after the launch.
Core Lightning developers are keeping the technical details of the vulnerabilities under embargo for two weeks.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission did not comment specifically on the discussions.
The Bitcoin ETF successfully integrated Bitcoin into traditional brokerage accounts.
properties.When to use:
1. A pronoun with no antecedent inside the claim ("He said ...", "its predecessor", "they announced") makes the claim Context-dependent.
2. A definite reference that needs an outside antecedent to identify it ("the vulnerabilities", "the discussions", "the recording", "the settlement terms", "the legal dispute", "recent actions") makes the claim Context-dependent, even when other entities in the claim are named.
3. A descriptive definite that names a kind of thing but not which one ("the Bitcoin ETF", "the major-bank stablecoin consortium", "the open-access version", "the infrastructure", "the new model") makes the claim Context-dependent: the reader must already know which ETF, consortium, version or product is meant. Applies to countable things, not to abstract or mass nouns ("the regulatory clearance", "the market").
4. Test: could a reader who sees only this sentence say which specific thing each definite reference points at? If any answer is no, tag Context-dependent.
5. Do not use for indefinites, time expressions, generics, or definites the claim itself resolves.
